subject: ela
description: Students compare and contrast two literary texts that are written in different forms or genres (for example, a story and a poem, or a historical novel and a fantasy story) by examining how each one approaches a similar theme or topic. They identify the shared theme or topic across both texts, then explain how each text's form, structure, language, and point of view shapes its particular approach to that theme. They describe what the two texts have in common and how they differ in the way they develop, deliver, or comment on the shared idea. Because this is a reading standard, every item embeds the full text of both passages or excerpts it depends on, so the student needs nothing external to answer.
subSkills: Identify the form or genre of each text (for example, story, poem, drama, myth, historical fiction, fantasy) and name a defining feature of that form
Determine the shared theme or topic that two texts in different forms both address
Describe how each text approaches the shared theme through its form, structure, language, imagery, or point of view
Compare the two texts: state what is similar in how they treat the theme or topic
Contrast the two texts: state how they differ in their approach, tone, emphasis, or message about the theme
Use specific evidence from both embedded texts to support each comparison or contrast

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the shared theme across forms
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short poem and short story embedded in the item, then name the theme or topic both texts explore: 'Both the poem and the story are mostly about what shared idea?' Answer names the theme (for example, the courage it takes to leave home) that appears in both texts regardless of their different forms.

problemArchetypes.name: Match an approach to its text
problemArchetypes.example: Read both embedded texts, then decide which text takes a stated approach: 'Which text uses vivid imagery and short lines to make the reader feel the loss quickly, and which builds the same feeling slowly through events?' Answer correctly attributes each approach to the poem or the story based on its form.

problemArchetypes.name: Compare how two forms treat the same topic
problemArchetypes.example: Read a fantasy excerpt and a historical-fiction excerpt embedded in the item that share a topic, then state one way they are alike in how they treat it: 'Both excerpts show a young hero facing an unfair rule. How is the way they present that struggle similar?' Answer names a genuine similarity supported by both texts.

problemArchetypes.name: Contrast how two forms treat the same topic
problemArchetypes.example: Read both embedded texts, then state one clear difference in approach: 'How does the poem's view of friendship differ from the story's view of friendship?' Answer names a real contrast in tone, emphasis, or message and points to evidence in each text.

problemArchetypes.name: Effect of form on the message
problemArchetypes.example: Read the poem and the story embedded in the item, then explain how each form shapes the theme: 'How does the poem's structure (its rhythm and repeated line) deliver the theme differently than the story's plot does?' Answer connects a feature of the form to the way the theme reaches the reader.

problemArchetypes.name: Evidence-supported comparison statement
problemArchetypes.example: Read both embedded texts, then choose the statement that accurately compares them and is backed by both: 'Which statement about the two texts is supported by evidence in each one?' Answer is the comparison that both texts actually justify, not one that fits only a single text.

Easy.description: Two very short texts in clearly different forms (for example, a four to six line poem and an 80 to 110 word story passage), both embedded in the item, that share an obvious, plainly stated theme or topic. The task is to identify: name the shared theme, name the form of each text, or match a directly stated feature to the correct text. The shared theme and the contrast are signaled on the surface; little inference is required.
constraints: Two short stimuli in different forms (a short poem of about 4 to 6 lines plus a story passage of about 80 to 110 words) included in the prompt
Shared theme or topic is concrete and stated or strongly signaled in both texts
Identify-level or match-level task: name the shared theme, label each form, or match a stated feature to its text
Differences between the two texts are clear on the surface; no multi-step inference needed

Medium.description: Two moderate-length texts in different forms or genres (for example, a 6 to 12 line poem and a 140 to 220 word story or excerpt), both embedded in the item, that share a theme treated somewhat differently in each. The task requires analysis: explain how each text approaches the shared theme through its form, state a genuine similarity or difference in approach, or connect a feature of the form to its effect. The answer is supported by both texts but is not stated word for word.
constraints: Two stimuli in different forms (a poem of about 6 to 12 lines plus a prose passage of about 140 to 220 words) included in the prompt
Shared theme is present in both but developed through different form features such as imagery, structure, or point of view
Analyze-level task: explain how each text treats the theme, or name a similarity or difference and support it
Some inference required; the approach of each text is shown through its language and structure rather than stated outright

Hard.description: Two longer or more layered texts in distinctly different genres (for example, a 10 to 18 line poem and a 240 to 360 word excerpt of historical or fantasy fiction), both embedded in the item, whose shared theme is treated with real divergence in tone, emphasis, or message. The task requires evaluation and synthesis: judge which text's approach better fits a stated purpose, explain how the contrast in form leads to a contrast in the message the reader takes away, or build a comparison that weighs evidence from several parts of each text. Requires sustained inference across both texts.
constraints: Two longer stimuli in clearly different genres (a poem of about 10 to 18 lines plus a prose excerpt of about 240 to 360 words) included in the prompt
Shared theme is treated with meaningful differences in tone, emphasis, or message across the two forms
Evaluate or synthesize task: judge or explain how the difference in form produces a difference in meaning, or build an evidence-weighted comparison
Requires inference that draws on evidence from several places in both embedded texts

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student analyzes only one of the two texts and treats that single text's approach as if it described both
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that accurately describes one text but is not true of the other, ignoring that the question asks about both

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student names a surface detail the two texts share (a word, a character age, a place) and mistakes it for a shared theme
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a shared concrete detail as the answer instead of the underlying theme or topic both texts actually explore

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes texts in different forms must disagree, and labels a real similarity as a difference
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks an answer that frames the two texts as opposite in their message when both texts in fact treat the theme in a similar way

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the form or genre of the two texts, attributing a poem's feature to the story or the story's feature to the poem
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Matches an approach or feature to the wrong text, swapping which one uses imagery and short lines and which one uses plot and events

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student states a comparison that sounds reasonable but is supported by neither embedded text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a plausible-sounding contrast that has no evidence in either passage

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student notices a difference in form but fails to connect it to how the theme or message reaches the reader
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks an answer that names a formal feature (rhyme, line breaks, dialogue) without linking it to any difference in how the theme is delivered

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks the approach that fits a stated purpose for the wrong text, reversing which form better serves the goal
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Identifies the text whose approach does not match the stated purpose, swapping the roles of the two forms
